JOHANNESBURG, South Africa (CNN) -- Ten South African ministers and the deputy president have resigned as President Thabo Mbeki prepares to leave office. South African President Thabo Mbeki announced his resignation in a televised address Sunday. His replacement, African National Congress Deputy President Kgalema Motlanthe, will be sworn in as South Africa's president Thursday. Mbeki announced he was resigning on Sunday, prompting threats from several Cabinet members to follow suit -- but the outgoing president urged them to stay in office, government sources said. The resignations, which include Finance Minister Trevor Manuel and Defense Minister Mosiuoa Lekota, will take effect Thursday when Mbeki steps down, a government statement said. "All the ministers have expressed their availability to assist the incoming administration in the hand-over process and any other assistance that might be sought from them," the statement said. The finance minister's assistant told CNN that Manuel is willing to serve in the new government, if needed. Three deputy ministers have also tendered their resignations, a government statement said. A spokesman for South Africa's ruling party, the African National Congress, confirmed that it has named Motlanthe as its choice to succeed Mbeki. Motlanthe will stay in office until elections in the spring of next year, which ANC President Jacob Zuma is widely expected to win. Earlier this month, the ANC asked Mbeki to step down after a judge threw out the corruption, fraud and racketeering case against Zuma -- Mbeki's political arch rival. The judge called the case invalid and accused Mbeki's government of political interference. Mbeki -- who has been South Africa's president for nearly 10 years -- spoke of some of his achievements when he formally announced his resignation on Sunday during a televised address.  Watch the significance of Mbeki "falling on the sword" » . "I depart this office knowing that many men and woman in South Africa have worked to achieve better lives for all," Mbeki said. Under his leadership the country has had the longest period of sustained economic growth in the South Africa's history and has reached out to indigent people in an unprecedented way, Mbeki said. Mbeki said the country still has economic, corruption and crime challenges to face in the future. And he gave his vote of confidence to the country's next leader without naming who that leader would be. Gwede Mantashe, secretary-general of the African National Congress, announced Saturday that the party -- which Mbeki has been involved with since his teens -- had asked him to leave before his term was up. Mbeki agreed to do so, he said. Mantashe said the ANC made the decision "for the citizens of South Africa, so there could be stability within the country" and so the ANC movement could remain "stable and unified." The case against Zuma -- who replaced Mbeki as ANC president last year -- was thrown out in September 2006, but the National Prosecuting Authority recharged him. Judge Chris Nicholson made no ruling on Zuma's guilt or innocence, and he could be recharged. Political observers doubted that would happen because of Zuma's popularity, particularly with the Communist Party and trade unions. Zuma has denied the charges. He said the case was politically motivated, and harmed his chances to become the ANC's presidential nominee. He could have faced at least 15 years in jail if convicted of accepting bribes from a company that got a contract in a multibillion-dollar arms deal. He also faced charges of having a corrupt relationship with his former financial adviser, Schabir Shaik, who is serving a 15-year sentence for soliciting bribes for Zuma and using Zuma's political influence to benefit his businesses. Mbeki, 66, succeeded Nelson Mandela as South Africa's president in June 1999. Critics alleged he pushed for the corruption charges against Zuma. Mbeki recently brokered a power-sharing deal between Zimbabwe's political rivals, who signed the agreement on Monday in an effort to put aside the violent past and end the crisis that has paralyzed Zimbabwe since disputed national elections in March. Under it, longtime Zimbabwean leader Robert Mugabe remains president, while his perennial rival, Morgan Tsvangirai, has become prime minister and the coordinator of government affairs.

"All the ministers have expressed their availability to assist the incoming administration in the hand-over process and any other assistance that might be sought from them," the statement read. Furthermore, an assistant to the finance minister informed CNN that Manuel remains willing to serve in the new government if called upon.

A spokesperson for the ruling ANC confirmed that the party has selected Motlanthe to succeed Mbeki. Motlanthe will serve as interim president until national elections next spring, which ANC President Jacob Zuma is widely expected to win. 

The political upheaval comes after the ANC requested Mbeki’s resignation earlier this month, following a judge’s dismissal of corruption, fraud, and racketeering charges against Zuma—Mbeki’s chief political rival. Presiding Judge Chris Nicholson declared the case invalid and accused Mbeki’s administration of political interference. ANC Secretary-General Gwede Mantashe stated on Saturday that the party—with which Mbeki has been affiliated since his teenage years—asked him to vacate the presidency early "for the citizens of South Africa, so there could be stability within the country" and to ensure the ANC remains "stable and unified." Mbeki agreed to the party's request.

The legal proceedings against Zuma, who replaced Mbeki as ANC president last year, have a complex history. Charges were initially thrown out in September 2006 before the National Prosecuting Authority recharged him. While Judge Nicholson made no explicit ruling on Zuma's guilt or innocence—leaving open the theoretical possibility of future prosecution—political analysts consider new charges unlikely given Zuma's formidable popular support, particularly among trade unions and the South African Communist Party. 

Zuma has consistently denied all allegations, asserting that the case was politically motivated to derail his presidential ambitions. "I depart this office knowing that many men and women in South Africa have worked to achieve better lives for all," Mbeki said. While acknowledging that South Africa must still confront significant economic, crime, and corruption challenges in the future, Mbeki expressed full confidence in the nation's next leader, though he refrained from naming a specific individual.

In addition to his domestic legacy, Mbeki recently brokered a landmark power-sharing agreement between Zimbabwe’s political rivals, signed on Monday. The deal aims to move past a violent political history and resolve the crisis that has paralyzed Zimbabwe since disputed national elections in March. Under the terms of the accord, longtime leader Robert Mugabe remains president, while his chief rival, Morgan Tsvangirai, assumes the role of prime minister and coordinator of government affairs.

The announcement followed a formal request from the ruling African National Congress (ANC) to recall him from office, plunging the nation's leadership into a period of swift transition.

**Johannesburg: The Beating Heart of South Africa**

Known affectionately to locals as Joburg, Jozi, or *eGoli*—the Zulu word for "City of Gold"—Johannesburg is a dynamic metropolis that serves as the economic engine and cultural heart of South Africa. Perched on the high-altitude plateau of the Highveld, it is a city forged from gold, shaped by a complex history, and fueled by an undeniable, relentless energy.

### A Golden Origin and Historic Legacy
Johannesburg’s story began in 1886 with the discovery of gold on the Witwatersrand ridge. Almost overnight, a dusty tent town transformed into a bustling boomtown, drawing fortune seekers from every corner of the globe. This rapid growth set the stage for South Africa’s industrialization, but it also laid the groundwork for deep social inequalities.

During the 20th century, Johannesburg became a key battleground in the fight against Apartheid. Today, the city honors its powerful past through world-class historical sites. The **Apartheid Museum** offers a profound, immersive journey into South Africa’s struggle for freedom. Just a short drive away lies **Soweto** (South Western Townships), a vibrant community rich in history. Here, visitors can walk down Vilakazi Street—the only street in the world once home to two Nobel Peace Prize laureates: Nelson Mandela and Archbishop Desmond Tutu.

### A Cultural Renaissance
In the 21st century, Johannesburg has undergone a massive creative rebirth. It is a melting pot of pan-African culture, where tradition seamlessly blends with modern innovation. Urban regeneration projects have transformed once-neglected industrial neighborhoods into thriving artistic hubs. 

The **Maboneng Precinct** and **Braamfontein** are glowing examples of this transformation. These districts buzz with street art, independent galleries, rooftop bars, and designer boutiques. On weekends, markets like the *Neighbourgoods Market* bring together foodies and fashion enthusiasts, celebrating the rich culinary and stylistic diversity of the African continent.

Johannesburg is also the undisputed capital of African music. From the birth of *Kwaito* in the 1990s to the global explosion of *Amapiano* today, the city’s nightlife vibrates with infectious rhythms that echo through its world-renowned clubs and live music venues.

### The World’s Largest Urban Forest
Despite its reputation as a concrete jungle and financial powerhouse, Johannesburg is surprisingly green. It is widely recognized as one of the largest man-made urban forests in the world, boasting over ten million trees. Parks like Emmarentia Dam, the Walter Sisulu National Botanical Garden, and the leafy suburbs of the Northern Suburbs provide lush, tranquil escapes from the fast-paced city life.

Just beyond the city limits lies the **Cradle of Humankind**, a UNESCO World Heritage Site containing some of the oldest hominid fossils ever discovered, connecting Johannesburg not just to the history of South Africa, but to the origin story of all humanity.

### The Spirit of Jozi
Johannesburg is a city of contrasts—raw yet refined, challenging yet deeply welcoming. Unlike coastal destinations that rely on natural beaches, Joburg thrives on its human capital. Its people are famously warm, resilient, and driven by a unique spirit of hustle and optimism. 

More than just a transit point for travelers on their way to a safari, Johannesburg is a destination of profound depth. It is a city that captures the raw, kinetic energy of modern Africa—a place where history was written, and where the continent's future is actively being shaped.

Here is a detailed news summary of the dramatic political events of September 2008 in South Africa, which saw the historic downfall of President Thabo Mbeki and a wave of high-profile cabinet resignations.

---

# SPECIAL REPORT: The 2008 Resignation of Thabo Mbeki and the ANC Cabinet Crisis

**DATELINE:** Johannesburg / Cape Town — September 2008  
**CONTEXT:** In September 2008, South Africa experienced its greatest political crisis since the end of apartheid. Thabo Mbeki, who had served as President since succeeding Nelson Mandela in 1999, was forced out of office by his own ruling party, the African National Congress (ANC). His removal triggered a wave of resignations from senior cabinet ministers, plunging the country into political uncertainty and causing short-term economic turbulence.

---

### 1. The Background: The ANC Power Struggle
The roots of the 2008 crisis lay in a bitter, years-long power struggle between President Thabo Mbeki and his former Deputy President, Jacob Zuma. 

* **2005:** Mbeki dismissed Zuma as Deputy President after Zuma’s financial advisor, Schabir Shaik, was convicted of corruption related to a massive 1999 state arms deal. Zuma was subsequently charged with corruption.
* **December 2007 (The Polokwane Conference):** At the ANC’s elective conference in Polokwane, a deeply divided party voted out Mbeki as ANC President and elected Jacob Zuma in his place. This created a dual center of power: Mbeki remained Head of State, but Zuma controlled the ruling party.

---

### 2. The Catalyst: Judge Nicholson’s Ruling
The immediate trigger for Mbeki’s downfall occurred on **September 12, 2008**. 

Pietermaritzburg High Court Judge Chris Nicholson dismissed corruption charges against Jacob Zuma on a legal technicality. Crucially, Judge Nicholson included obiter dicta (comments) in his ruling suggesting that Mbeki’s executive government had politically interfered in the decision by the National Prosecuting Authority (NPA) to prosecute Zuma.

Although Mbeki strongly denied these allegations, the Zuma-aligned leadership of the ANC used the judge's comments as the justification to move against the sitting president.

---

### 3. The "Recall" and Mbeki's Resignation
On **September 20, 2008**, following a grueling 14-hour meeting of the ANC’s National Executive Committee (NEC), party Secretary-General Gwede Mantashe officially announced that the ANC had decided to "recall" Mbeki from the presidency before his term officially ended in mid-2009.

**Mbeki’s Address to the Nation (September 21, 2008):**
* Respecting party discipline, Mbeki agreed to step down, tendering his resignation to the Speaker of Parliament.
* In a dignified, televised address, Mbeki defended his legacy, particularly his economic management and foreign policy.
* He explicitly rejected Judge Nicholson’s findings, stating: *"I would like to state this unequivocally: that we have never interfered with the work of the National Prosecuting Authority... This includes the painful matter relating to the prosecution of the President of the ANC, Comrade Jacob Zuma."*

*(Note: In 2009, the Supreme Court of Appeal unanimously overturned Judge Nicholson’s findings of political interference, but by then, Mbeki had already been removed.)*

---

### 4. The Cabinet Exodus and Financial Turmoil
On **September 23, 2008**, the crisis deepened when the Presidency announced that **11 cabinet ministers and three deputy ministers** had tendered their resignations out of loyalty to Mbeki or refusal to serve under the incoming faction.

#### Key Resignations Included:
* **Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka** (Deputy President)
* **Trevor Manuel** (Minister of Finance)
* **Alec Erwin** (Minister of Public Enterprises)
* **Ronnie Kasrils** (Minister of Intelligence)
* **Sydney Mufamadi** (Minister of Provincial and Local Government)
* **Nkosazana Dlamini-Zuma** (Minister of Home Affairs — though she later withdrew her resignation)

#### Market Panic over Trevor Manuel
The most damaging element of the exodus was the resignation of **Finance Minister Trevor Manuel**, who was highly revered by international investors for his fiscal discipline. 
* Upon news of his resignation, the South African Rand plummeted by nearly 4% against the US Dollar, and the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE) suffered sharp losses.
* **The Clarification:** Hours later, Manuel’s spokesperson clarified that his resignation was a constitutional formality (as ministers serve at the pleasure of the outgoing President) and that Manuel was entirely willing to serve under the new administration. The markets subsequently stabilized.

---

### 5. The Transition: Kgalema Motlanthe Steps In
To ensure stability ahead of the scheduled 2009 general election, the ANC selected **Kgalema Motlanthe**—then Deputy President of the ANC and a respected, unifying figure—to serve as caretaker President.

* On **September 25, 2008**, Parliament officially elected Motlanthe as President of South Africa.
* Motlanthe immediately re-appointed Trevor Manuel as Finance Minister and retained several other resigning ministers to signal continuity and calm domestic and foreign markets.

---

### 6. The Broader Impact and Legacy

1. **Formation of COPE:** Disillusioned by Mbeki’s ousted faction and the growing dominance of Zuma, several prominent ANC leaders (including former Defense Minister Mosiuoa Lekota and former Gauteng Premier Mbhazima Shilowa) broke away to form a new opposition party, the **Congress of the People (COPE)**, in late 2008.
2. **Clearance for Jacob Zuma:** The removal of Mbeki effectively paved the way for Jacob Zuma to assume the presidency following the April 2009 general election, inaugurating a controversial nine-year era in South African politics marked by state capture allegations.
3. **Constitutional Precedent:** The event established a powerful precedent in South African politics: that the ANC leadership committee (the NEC) held more practical power over the nation's Executive than Parliament itself, capable of removing a sitting Head of State mid-term—a maneuver the party would repeat a decade later with Jacob Zuma himself in 2018.

**POLITICAL EARTHQUAKE IN SOUTH AFRICA: PRESIDENT THABO MBEKI RESIGNS AMID BITTER ANC POWER STRUGGLE**

**JOHANNESBURG, South Africa (CNN)** — In a dramatic and historic turn of events, South African President Thabo Mbeki has formally announced his resignation, plunging the continent's largest economy into its worst political crisis since the fall of apartheid. 

Mbeki’s televised address to the nation on Sunday night followed a grueling, 14-hour meeting of the ruling African National Congress (ANC) Executive Committee, which voted to "recall" the sitting president seven months before his second term was set to end. 

"I have tendered my resignation to the Speaker of the National Assembly," a solemn Mbeki said, maintaining his signature composure. "I have served our country to the best of my ability."

### THE SPARK: THE ZUMA LEGAL SAGA

The immediate catalyst for Mbeki’s historic downfall is a explosive High Court ruling regarding his arch-rival and the current president of the ANC, Jacob Zuma. 

Zuma, a charismatic populist with deep support among South Africa’s working class and trade unions, has been locked in a years-long legal battle over allegations of corruption, fraud, and racketeering linked to a 1999 multi-billion-dollar government arms deal. 

Last week, High Court Judge Chris Nicholson threw out the corruption charges against Zuma on a technicality. However, the judge went a step further, delivering a blistering judgment that implied Mbeki’s administration had engaged in high-level "political interference" to weaponize the National Prosecuting Authority (NPA) against Zuma.

Though Mbeki vehemently denied the allegations of political meddling—calling them "categorically untrue"—Zuma’s allies within the ANC seized the moment. Meeting in the outskirts of Johannesburg, the party leadership executed a swift political coup, demanding Mbeki step down.

"This is not a matter of revenge; it is a matter of healing the party," said ANC Secretary-General Gwede Mantashe in a press conference following the decision.

### MOTLANTHE STEPS INTO THE BREACH

To prevent a power vacuum, the ANC has announced that Kgalema Motlanthe, the deputy president of the party and a highly respected former trade unionist, will serve as interim president. 

Motlanthe, viewed as a calm, unifying figure, is expected to be sworn in by Parliament later this week. His primary directive will be to steady the ship and reassure jittery international markets until national elections take place in mid-2009—elections that Jacob Zuma is widely expected to win.

Despite Motlanthe's appointment, the political shockwaves are reverberating through the country’s financial centers. The South African Rand tumbled against the US dollar following news of Mbeki's resignation, driven by fears that Mbeki's investor-friendly, fiscally conservative economic policies might be dismantled in favor of Zuma’s left-leaning platform.

### A TALE OF TWO LEGACIES: DOMESTIC DOWNFALL VS. INTERNATIONAL TOWER

Mbeki’s abrupt exit marks a tragic end to a complex political career. While his domestic legacy has been tarnished by a sluggish response to crime, controversy over HIV/AIDS policies, and his bitter feud with Zuma, his foreign policy legacy remains towering.

Mbeki was widely regarded as the chief architect of the "African Renaissance"—a vision of a self-reliant continent driven by democratic governance and economic integration. 

Among his crowning foreign policy achievements:

*   **Architect of NEPAD and the African Union:** Mbeki was instrumental in transforming the old Organization of African Unity (OAU) into the modern African Union (AU) in 2002, and he launched the New Partnership for Africa’s Development (NEPAD) to attract Western investment in exchange for good governance.
*   **Peacekeeper and Mediator:** Mbeki deployed South African troops on key peacekeeping missions across the continent, including Burundi and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).
*   **The Zimbabwe Breakthrough:** Just days before his resignation, Mbeki scored a major diplomatic victory by brokering a power-sharing agreement between Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe and opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai, ending a deadly political deadlock in neighboring Zimbabwe.

"On the world stage, Thabo Mbeki was a titan," noted CNN Senior International Correspondent Christiane Amanpour. "He raised South Africa's diplomatic profile, demanding a seat at the table with the G8 and securing a temporary seat on the UN Security Council. But while he was solving Africa's problems abroad, the ground was shifting beneath his feet at home."

### A DEMOCRACY TESTED

As South Africa prepares for a new administration, the country finds itself at a critical crossroads. Rumors are already swirling that Mbeki loyalists within the cabinet may resign in protest, and a faction of the ANC is threatening to break away to form a new opposition party—a move that would fundamentally alter South Africa's political landscape for the first time since 1994.

For now, the nation holds its breath. Nelson Mandela’s party, once a monolithic liberation movement, stands deeply divided, and the transition from the cerebral statesman Thabo Mbeki to the populist Jacob Zuma has begun in earnest. 

*CNN’s David McKenzie contributed to this report from Johannesburg.*

counterfactuals.prompt: What happened when Thabo Mbeki resigned as president of South Africa? Include details about which ministers quit and why the ANC asked him to step down.
counterfactuals.output:
In September 2008, South African President Thabo Mbeki announced his resignation after the ruling African National Congress (ANC) formally asked him to step down ("recalled" him). His resignation marked one of the most dramatic political shifts in South Africa’s post-apartheid history.

Here is a detailed breakdown of why the ANC asked him to step down, what happened when he resigned, and which ministers quit.

---

### 1. Why the ANC Asked Mbeki to Step Down

The decision to recall Mbeki was the culmination of a bitter, years-long power struggle between Mbeki and his former deputy president, **Jacob Zuma**. 

* **The Mbeki-Zuma Rift:** In 2005, Mbeki dismissed Zuma as Vice President after Zuma's financial advisor, Schabir Shaik, was convicted of corruption. This created a deep divide within the ANC. Zuma’s supporters argued that the corruption charges against him were politically motivated by Mbeki’s camp.
* **The Polokwane Conference (2007):** In December 2007, Zuma defeated Mbeki in the election for the presidency of the ANC. This created a dual power structure: Mbeki was President of South Africa, but Zuma was President of the ANC. 
* **The Tipping Point (Judge Nicholson’s Ruling):** On September 12, 2008, High Court Judge Chris Nicholson dismissed corruption charges against Jacob Zuma on procedural grounds. Crucially, the judge stated there was evidence of "political interference" by Mbeki’s administration and cabinet in the National Prosecuting Authority’s (NPA) decision to prosecute Zuma. 
* **The NEC Vote:** The ruling gave Zuma’s allies in the ANC the leverage they needed. On September 20, 2008, the ANC’s National Executive Committee (NEC) voted to recall Mbeki. Though the South African Constitution does not give a political party the direct power to remove a sitting president, Mbeki chose not to fight the decision in Parliament and agreed to resign to maintain party stability.

---

### 2. What Happened When He Resigned

* **Televised Address:** On September 21, 2008, Mbeki delivered a dignified, televised address to the nation, officially announcing his resignation effective upon the appointment of his successor. He denied allegations that he had interfered in the judicial process or targeted Zuma.
* **Interim Leadership:** Parliament formally accepted Mbeki's resignation on September 25. **Kgalema Motlanthe**, the deputy president of the ANC, was sworn in as interim President of South Africa to serve until the general election in May 2009 (at which point Jacob Zuma became president).
* **Court Vindication (Too Late):** Months later, in January 2009, the Supreme Court of Appeal overturned Judge Nicholson’s findings regarding executive interference, calling them "speculative" and "unwarranted." However, by then, Mbeki had already been removed from office.

---

### 3. Which Ministers Quit

Mbeki’s resignation triggered a wave of resignations within his Cabinet. A total of **11 cabinet ministers and 3 deputy ministers** tendered their resignations out of loyalty to Mbeki, unwillingness to serve under a Zuma-led ANC, or constitutional protocol.

#### Key Ministers Who Resigned:
1. **Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka** – Deputy President of South Africa.
2. **Trevor Manuel** – Minister of Finance. *(His resignation caused an immediate panic in the financial markets, sending the South African Rand tumbling and stocks dropping. However, Manuel quickly clarified that he resigned out of constitutional procedure and was willing to serve under the next administration; he was reappointed almost immediately).*
3. **Mosiuoa "Terror" Lekota** – Minister of Defence (he later broke away from the ANC entirely).
4. **Alec Erwin** – Minister of Public Enterprises.
5. **Ronnie Kasrils** – Minister of Intelligence Services.
6. **Geraldine Fraser-Moleketi** – Minister of Public Service and Administration.
7. **Sydney Mufamadi** – Minister of Provincial and Local Government.
8. **Buyelwa Sonjica** – Minister of Water Affairs and Forestry.
9. **Aziz Pahad** – Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs.

---

### 4. Aftermath and Impact

* **Political Split (Formation of COPE):** Disgruntled Mbeki loyalists, led by former Defence Minister Mosiuoa Lekota and former Gauteng Premier Mbhazima Shilowa, broke away from the ANC to form a new political party called the **Congress of the People (COPE)**. This was the first major breakaway party from the ANC since 1994.
* **Shift to the Zuma Era:** Mbeki’s departure cemented Jacob Zuma's control over the ANC and the state, leading directly to Zuma assuming the presidency in May 2009. 
* **Constitutional Precedent:** Mbeki's recall established a precedent in South African politics—that the ruling party could force a sitting country president to step down. This same mechanism was used a decade later, in February 2018, when the ANC forced Jacob Zuma to resign.

**POLITICAL EARTHQUAKE IN PRETORIA: SOUTH AFRICA’S PRESIDENT RESIGNS ALONGSIDE 10 CABINET MINISTERS**

**PRETORIA, South Africa** — In an unprecedented political crisis that has sent shockwaves across the African continent and international financial markets, South Africa’s President announced his resignation late Thursday evening, accompanied by the dramatic walkout of ten high-ranking cabinet ministers. 

The mass resignation follows months of mounting public fury over a worsening energy crisis, stagnant economic growth, and high-level corruption allegations that fractured the ruling coalition beyond repair. 

Addressing the nation in a tense, televised broadcast from the Union Buildings in Pretoria, the President stated that his departure was "in the best interest of national stability."

"It has become clear that the current political impasse is hindering our ability to govern effectively and serve the people of South Africa," the President said. "To allow the nation to heal, reconstitute, and move forward with clarity, I have tendered my resignation to the Speaker of the National Assembly, effective immediately."

Within minutes of the address, a joint statement confirmed that ten cabinet ministers—including those holding crucial portfolios in Finance, Energy, Public Enterprises, and Police—had also tendered their resignations. Sources close to the administration described a frantic afternoon of closed-door meetings where ministers allied with the President chose to step down en masse rather than face a planned vote of no confidence in Parliament next week.

### **A Nation in Shock**

The dramatic collapse of the executive branch marks the most significant political upheaval in South Africa since the end of apartheid in 1994. 

The South African Rand (ZAR) plummeted nearly 4% against the U.S. Dollar within hours of the announcement, reflecting deep market anxiety over the sudden leadership vacuum. Sovereign bond yields also spiked as global rating agencies warned of potential credit rating downgrades.

Outside the Parliamentary precinct in Cape Town and in the streets of Johannesburg, crowds gathered late into the night. While opposition supporters celebrated what they termed "the end of a failed era," many citizens expressed deep anxiety over the political instability ahead.

"We are entering uncharted waters," said Dr. Thabo Mthembu, a senior political analyst at the University of the Witwatersrand. "A presidential resignation is not unprecedented in South Africa, but the simultaneous departure of ten cabinet ministers strips the government of its core executive authority overnight. It creates an institutional crisis we haven't seen in 30 years."

### **Constitutional Next Steps**

Under the South African Constitution, the Deputy President automatically assumes the role of Acting President until Parliament can convene. 

The Speaker of the National Assembly confirmed midnight Thursday that an emergency parliamentary session would be called within the next seven days. Parliament will be tasked with electing a new President from among its members to serve out the remainder of the term.

However, major opposition parties are already rallying to demand more than just a leadership swap within the ruling party. Opposition leaders have called for the immediate dissolution of Parliament and the scheduling of snap national elections.

"The resignation of the President and his ministers is a clear admission of failure," said the chief leader of the official opposition. "The ruling party cannot simply shuffle the deck chairs on a sinking ship. The people of South Africa deserve the right to choose an entirely new government."

### **Uncertain Future**

The resignations leave key government departments without political heads at a critical juncture. The Department of Public Enterprises, currently managing the restructuring of state-owned entities, and the National Treasury, which was scheduled to present the mid-term budget policy statement next month, are now functioning purely under bureaucratic administration.

The Acting President is expected to address the nation on Friday morning to announce an interim cabinet aimed at stabilizing the financial markets and restoring order to government operations. 

For now, South Africa stands at a monumental crossroads, with its democratic institutions facing their greatest test in modern history.

### **MBEKI RECALLED: ANC FORCES PRESIDENT OUT AFTER JUDGE FINDS POLITICAL MEDDLING IN ZUMA CASE**

**JOHANNESBURG (SAPA)** — In an unprecedented political earthquake that marks the end of the post-Mandela era, the African National Congress (ANC) National Executive Committee (NEC) has formally requested the immediate resignation of South African President Thabo Mbeki. 

The extraordinary decision, announced Saturday afternoon by ANC Secretary-General Gwede Mantashe following a marathon, closed-door meeting at the St. George’s Hotel in Irene, Pretoria, follows eight days of intense internal turmoil sparked by a bombshell High Court ruling in Pietermaritzburg.

On September 12, Judge Chris Nicholson dismissed corruption charges against ANC President Jacob Zuma, ruling that the decision by the National Prosecuting Authority (NPA) to recharge Zuma was procedurally invalid. Crucially, Nicholson suggested that top members of Mbeki’s cabinet—and implicitly Mbeki himself—had engaged in political "executive interference" to weaponize the justice system against Zuma.

Mantashe added that Mbeki had accepted the decision "without a fight" and would follow constitutional procedures to tender his resignation to Parliament.

### **A DEEPENING FACTIONAL SPLIT**

The recall of Mbeki is the dramatic culmination of a bitter power struggle that has consumed the ruling party since December 2007, when Zuma decisively ousted Mbeki as ANC leader at the party’s historic Polokwane conference. 

Since the Polokwane defeat, Mbeki’s authority as head of state had grown increasingly fragile, creating a bizarre dual power structure in South African politics: Mbeki leading the government from Union Buildings, and Zuma wielding political power from Luthuli House.

The Nicholson ruling destroyed the delicate stalemate. In his 148-page judgment, Judge Nicholson stated that he was "not satisfied that the political background to this matter can be ignored," explicitly linking the timing of Zuma’s prosecution to Mbeki’s attempt to secure a third term as party president.

The findings catalyzed immediate calls for Mbeki’s removal from the ANC’s Left wing, including the South African Communist Party (SACP), the Congress of South African Trade Unions (COSATU), and the ANC Youth League, led by Julius Malema.

### **CONSTITUTIONAL CRISIS AND MARKET ANXIETY**

Mbeki’s impending resignation plunges South Africa into unfamiliar legal and economic territory. Under Section 86 of the Constitution, the Cabinet will technically dissolve once the President resigns, requiring Parliament to elect a new President from among its members within 30 days.

Mantashe attempted to quell fears on Saturday, assuring the public that economic policy would remain unchanged.

### **WHAT NEXT FOR ZUMA?**

While Mbeki’s political career comes to a sudden and ignominious end, Jacob Zuma emerges from the saga triumphant. Though the NPA has indicated it may appeal Judge Nicholson’s ruling, the political momentum is now overwhelmingly behind the charismatic 66-year-old leader.

Zuma, who was fired by Mbeki as the country's Deputy President in 2005 following the corruption conviction of his financial advisor Schabir Shaik, is now virtually guaranteed to assume the Presidency of South Africa following the 2009 general election.
